Algeria Implements Sweeping Import Restrictions, Sparking Disruption Across Sectors

Algiers – Algeria’s sweeping new import restrictions, announced last week and already in partial effect, are sending ripples across the nation’s economy, affecting companies from heavy industry to local retailers. The measure, which imposes broad limits on the import of a wide range of goods, has prompted concern among business leaders and analysts as supply chains grow strained and costs begin to rise.

The government’s decision, delivered via executive decree on Sunday, prohibits the import of dozens of categories including machinery, spare parts, electronics, and certain food products. Officials say the policy aims to protect domestic producers and address the country’s persistent trade deficit. “Algeria must reduce reliance on foreign goods and build a resilient local economy,” said Minister of Commerce Abdelkader Cherif in a statement on Tuesday. “These measures are temporary but necessary.”

Societe Nationale de I Electricite & Du Gaz SpA, Algeria’s state-owned utility, is among the companies already feeling the impact. “Several vital components for our maintenance and expansion projects are currently delayed at ports due to the new restrictions,” a spokesperson for the company told reporters. “We are assessing inventory and working with authorities to avoid interruptions in service to our customers.”

Industrial groups say the restrictions are affecting their ability to maintain operations. “Without access to specialized equipment and replacement parts, production lines are at risk of stalling,” said Mourad Belkacem, chair of the Algerian Manufacturers’ Union. “We urge the government to clarify which goods will be allowed in under exemptions, especially items critical to national infrastructure.”

Small businesses are also expressing anxiety. Fatima Boudjemaa, who manages a consumer electronics shop in Oran, says her shelves are already thinning. “Customers ask for items we can no longer order. We’re worried about keeping the business open through the summer,” she said.

Analysts warn that the restrictions could push up prices and slow economic growth if maintained over the long term. “The intention behind these policies is understandable, but the risk is that Algeria’s domestic industries are not yet ready to fill the gap,” said economic analyst Yacine Abdelmoumene. “If shortages persist, we could see inflation accelerate and investment decisions delayed.”

Authorities say they are monitoring the situation closely and promise further guidance in the coming days. Meanwhile, business leaders and ordinary Algerians alike are bracing for the continuing effects as the trade policy remains in place.
